#1050. Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

#1048. Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

Eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”

This was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and said “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

The anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

It was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

#1044. Cesc Fabregas's Como win NINE-ONE in the biggest away victory in Champions League history - two weeks after thrashing Michael Carrick's Man United - in just their first year at Europe's top table

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and LUKE POWER, SPORTS REPORTER

Published: 17:01 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 07:28 EDT, 5 November 2026

Manchester United's 4-1 battering by Como two weeks ago now looks a lucky escape – after the Italian side romped to a 9-1 victory at Lens in the Champions League.

Cesc Fabregas' side put in a stunning performance in a record-equalling win which well and truly announced them as contenders on the biggest stage.

Como now sit fourth in the Champions League standings after also thrashing RB Leipzig and Man United, who are likely relieved that Lens took such a pounding.

It means only Paris Saint-Germain, Real Madrid, and Arsenal have got off to better starts, despite this being their maiden season in European competition.

The lakeside outfit were 3-0 up at half-time – with the scorer of the third goal, Nico Paz, paying his respects to late Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel – before a rout after the break.

It is the latest statement win for Como, whose transformation began in 2019 when a pair of Indonesian billionaire brothers, who originally made their fortune in the tobacco industry, bought the club for $850,000 (£644,427) through their Djarum Group.

Como thrashed Lens 9-1 in a record-equalling victory in the Champions League on Wednesday

Cesc Fabregas is quickly building his name as one of the most talented coaches in Europe

With a combined net worth then estimated at $48billion (£36.4billion), Robert Budi Hartono and Michael Bambang Hartono instantly made Como the richest club in Italian football.

Rather than pursue instant success through lavish spending, Como have built steadily, investing in infrastructure, recruitment, and a clear footballing identity – and it is paying off big-time.

They have now won six games on the bounce, though they still sit fourth in Serie A five points behind leaders Lazio, who have had an almost perfect start.

Their crushing of Lens was the first time an Italian side had scored seven or more goals away from home in European Cup/Champions League history.

And their hat-trick hero on the night, Anastasios Douvikas, is now the top scorer in the Champions League ahead of Erling Haaland.

All of this comes for a side who were playing in the third tier just six seasons ago and on the back of a relatively modest summer spend of £58million on nine permanent arrivals and loanees.

'Today everything went our way,' said an ecstatic Fabregas post-match. 'A great night for Como and our fans.'

There was a poignant moment when Paz paid homage to Miguel and his hometown club, holding aloft a shirt with the picture of the late star alongside the caption: 'Rest in peace.' Though he plays for Argentina, Paz was born in Tenerife and also spent time in the club's youth system from 2014-16.

Miguel died on Tuesday morning less than 24 hours after a collision with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during their Spanish second division match on Monday. Having suffered serious head and chest injuries he subsequently suffered a cardiac arrest.

Como's Nico Paz paid tribute to Jesus de Miguel during his goalscoring celebration vs Lens

Despite playing for Argentina, Paz was born in Tenerife and also played for their youth teams

Tenerife striker De Miguel died on Tuesday morning after a horrifying clash with Jesus Owono

Como led 3-0 at half-time with hat-trick hero Douvikas scoring two at that point before Paz's goal and his De Miguel tribute.

Soon after the interval the Serie A outfit crushed any notion of the hosts coming back as they plundered in five goals in a devastating 22-minute spell which included Douvikas completing his hat-trick. Lucas Da Cunha, Marc-Oliver Kempf, Mattia Liberali, Martina Baturina also got in on the act during that period.

Ruben Aguilar pulled one back for Lens before Matteo Papaccioli rounded off the rout in stoppage time. The 18-year-old Papaccioli, who came on in the second half, is a member of Como's youth team and hasn't even played in Serie A yet.

Wednesday's win means Como have broken many records in the Champions League.

The Italian side matched the eight-goal winning margins recorded by Liverpool and Real Madrid in their 8-0 home victories over Besiktas and Malmo respectively. They also became only the second team after Bayern Munich to score nine goals in a Champions League match.

Como followed their 4-1 victory over Manchester United with another emphatic performance, becoming the first team to score nine goals away from home in the European Cup since 1971 – Feyenoord beat Olympiacos Nicosia by this scoreline – as they climbed to fourth in the standings on nine points. The previous best scoring performance by an away club in the Champions League was Bayern Munich's 8-2 win over Barcelona at a neutral venue (Lisbon) in 2020.

Fabregas's side may have made Champions League record-equalling history, but Feyenoord hold the European Cup mark for most goals scored in a single match, having beaten Icelandic side KR 12-2 in September 1969.

Lens, who suffered the heaviest defeat by a French club in the competition, are 33rd with three points.

#1042. Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why

Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

Few national elections carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.

Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant.

Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.

"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.

"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."

The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.

For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation.

During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.

"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank Climate Analytics.

Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.

Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.

Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.

Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.

"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest,'" said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Center at London-based think tank Chatham House.

"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.

Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.

"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.

More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.

"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.

In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.

A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.

But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.

Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".

"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.

The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians climate is not high on their list of priorities.

"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.

"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.

#1041. When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Emma Marris is a writer in Portland, Oregon.

Life-sized puppets in a remote village in Japan symbolize depopulation in the country. Credit: Buddhika Weerasinghe/Getty

Less than an hour’s train ride from central Tokyo, ecologist Kei Uchida walks through glades of mountain cherry trees and meadows filled with susuki grass as tall as an elephant. The researcher smiles when he spots something by the trail: a tangled orb of grass stalks, at about knee height. It is the nest of the tiny Eurasian harvest mouse (Micromys minutus), a species that has been on the decline in this area and has been targeted for protection.

Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Volunteers saved this location around Mount Tenran from development 30 years ago, and today they monitor its plants and animals, thin its forests and even plant and harvest rice — all in the name of biodiversity. Here, nature needs people. In the shallow water of the rice paddy, fish as small and arched as an eyebrow swim, and just above the water’s surface, dragonflies mate. At dusk, fireflies dance above the fields.

Uchida, an environmental scientist at Tokyo City University in Yokohama, and his colleagues included this site in a study of thousands of species in more than 150 wooded, agricultural and ‘peri-urban’ landscapes in Japan1. Unsurprisingly, they found that the diversity and abundance of most species declined at sites where the human population was growing. But they also found that biodiversity declined in places where the number of people was decreasing (see ‘Lost life’). This result — and others like it in different parts of the world — contradicts the common assumption that when people leave, nature always thrives.

Japan and many other nations are seeing a vast emptying of rural areas as people flock towards urban centres. Studies2 are showing that this can have a detrimental effect on biodiversity in the depopulated areas, which creates new challenges. Rather than simply setting up and managing protected areas, conservation officials must consider whether and how to recruit, train and support people to be permanent parts of some ecosystems.

I’ve joined Uchida and local volunteers to learn more about how human activity can increase biodiversity. Uchida says that this area is a typical satoyama landscape — a term that combines the words for village and mountain. “Agriculture and living things can coexist,” Uchida says. But Japan’s satoyama are being lost to depopulation and urbanization.

In this area near Mount Tenran, as in many woodlands across Japan, humans spent centuries cutting trees for fuel and removing fallen leaves for fertilizer. That opened up the forest and benefited specific plants and insects. But when that activity stopped, the forest became dense and closed in again. “We have used the woods for 1,000 years, but not lately,” Uchida says. Now, young students are being given small handsaws and taught the centuries-old art of woodland thinning.

Kojima Tsubasa, a volunteer nature monitor, shows me where he sits in the evenings to count fireflies. There are two types here: the smaller heike fireflies (Aquatica lateralis), which prefer rice fields; and the larger, brighter genji fireflies (Nipponoluciola cruciata), associated with running streams. “It’s rare to see both at once,” he says, proudly. Four days ago, Tsubasa says, he counted 60 fireflies at this paddy. Often, he is not alone. Japanese urbanites, yearning for the charm of the countryside, come here to watch the fireflies at dusk. But after the show, they get on the train and return to the brighter lights of Tokyo.

Most Japanese people now have to travel to see fireflies — whereas once the insect’s bright beauty was right outside their homes. It’s a trend seen the world over. As recently as 1950, nearly 40% of the global human population lived in the countryside. According to United Nations data, just 19% of the world’s 8.2 billion people now live in rural areas. The global rural population is expected to peak in the 2040s and decline thereafter.

In some countries, that rural decline is well under way. Japan’s total population shrank by four million between 2015 and 2025, and the rural population is shrinking even faster. In 2025, just 8.6% of its population was classified as rural. Peter Matanle, an independent environmental social scientist who worked with Uchida on the biodiversity study, calls Japan a “vanguard country” that other nations can learn from when it comes to depopulation. European Union data, for example, show that between 2015 and 2024, rural areas in Europe lost 0.2% of their population per year. Furthermore, rural communities tend to have older populations than do urban communities, a harbinger of further depopulation.

Uchida and his co-authors studied the effects of this demographic shift by examining data on 464 species of bird, butterfly, firefly and frog as well as nearly 3,000 plant species collected in various landscapes across Japan over periods of 5–17 years, starting in 2004. They found that biodiversity declined in areas where there was greater disruption of the landscape — either by people moving in and building infrastructure or by agricultural intensification, in which corporate farms replace smaller, family-run operations.

Rewilding the planet: how seven artificial islands could help a dying Dutch lake

Rewilding the planet: how seven artificial islands could help a dying Dutch lake

They also documented declines in biodiversity in places abandoned by people. Although that might seem paradoxical, the researchers note that when irrigation ceases, amphibians and many insects can no longer reproduce; other ecological niches are lost as well. The resulting dry, abandoned landscape is too fragmented for many species to recolonize. “Leaving it alone isn’t doing anyone any good,” Matanle says.

Similar relationships between rural depopulation and biodiversity have been documented in Europe. A study of 70 sites in Albania, Bulgaria, Croatia and Greece found that rural abandonment in these countries had “a consistent negative effect on bird communities”2. The species hit hardest were those that populate farmlands, according to the researchers. A European Commission monitoring scheme found that populations of farmland birds in Europe declined by 58% between 1980 and 2024, as agriculture intensified in some locations and moved out of others.

Birds are not the only organisms that have thrived in human landscapes. In Sweden, ‘semi-natural grasslands’, which have been cleared by humans and are kept open by livestock, are prime habitat for one-third of the country’s threatened species, and can contain up to 40 plant species per square metre3. As people left the countryside after the Second World War and land use evolved away from extensive pastures, the total area of these grasslands decreased by more than 90% in some regions4. In many cases, the removal of grazers led to the land being converted to row crops or forest — due to either spontaneous growth of trees or intentional planting for timber. Both types of forest are less biodiverse than the semi-natural grasslands they replaced.

In Spain, ecologist Francisco Lloret, at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, says that as people leave the countryside, biodiversity falls because some species are losing habitat and others are losing food. Vultures and other scavengers, for example, have relied on livestock for centuries, but that source of food is disappearing.

A revolution is sweeping Europe’s farms: can it save agriculture?

A revolution is sweeping Europe’s farms: can it save agriculture?

Wooded or herbaceous areas on the edges of fields are also in decline. In Mediterranean countries such as Spain, fields are often bounded by herbaceous borders — or by dry stone walls, which shelter many vertebrates and invertebrates. When such walls are knocked down to make larger fields for modern agricultural systems that require fewer people, those organisms are lost.

Why do so many species thrive in low-intensity farming landscapes? The mechanisms behind the relationship vary from species to species, say researchers. Some organisms prefer the standing water of rice fields, some tend towards the grasslands kept open by mowing or livestock, and some thrive at the edge of a forest. But the overarching themes of research seem to be that many species rely on the maintenance of a mosaic of habitat types and regular, modest disturbance through activities such as seasonal flooding, livestock grazing, burning, thinning and patchy clearing. Inhabited landscapes that experience such disruptions often host more species than a large expanse of undisturbed forest does.

These are the Arcadian landscapes of the Romantic poets, of The Wind in the Willows (1908) and of My Neighbor Totoro: culturally beloved ecosystems that have supported a suite of species since at least the Iron Age. “Biodiversity has evolved in the last millennia with people and human activities,” Lloret says. Some species might even have evolved to fit better into human landscapes. However, Lloret cautions that there are no universal rules. Context is king. In some places, depopulation increases biodiversity. Top predators, such as wolves, often do best in places without people. In the tropics — home to the most biodiverse places on Earth — few countries are experiencing depopulation and habitat loss is a much greater concern.

In response to biodiversity losses linked to rural depopulation, a team of conservation researchers in the Czech Republic and Poland have called for small-scale farming as a conservation tool to save farmland birds5. As a bonus, such farming communities would provide “high aesthetic and heritage values”, the team argues. Uchida and his colleagues suggest “a new interventionist wilding” to complement rewilding efforts that seek to set up nature to run itself. Some schemes run by the EU aim to support farmers and biodiversity, but they’ve been criticized as being ineffective6.

After my hike with the volunteers and Uchida, we emerge from the forest just as the sky opens and rain begins to pour. We go to a nearby bakery for a Japanese snack called curry bread, and I ask the question that has been on my mind all day: who will do the work of creating habitats for vulnerable species in the countryside in the future?

Cristiano Ronaldo has called time on his illustrious career in international football.

Ronaldo, 41, scored a world record 146 goals in 234 games for Portugal and won the 2016 European Championship as well as two Nations League titles.

His retirement comes just weeks after his explosive falling-out with new manager Jorge Jesus, which ended with Ronaldo abandoning Portugal's camp during the most recent international break in September and October.

It appeared as if he could return for the upcoming break this month for clashes with Denmark and Wales, but he has decided to step away after 23 years.

In his retirement statement, he admitted that he had at times 'failed' and revealed that his decision was difficult, but felt proud of his work and willing to hand over the number seven jersey.

The Al-Nassr star is hoping to pass the baton to his son, 16-year-old Cristiano Junior, who this week has been called up for Portugal's Under-17s.

Ronaldo made his debut for Portugal in 2003 aged 18 and went on to play in six World Cups, a record he shares with Lionel Messi, as well as six European Championships, two Nations League finals, and a Confederations Cup.

Cristiano Ronaldo has called time on his illustrious international career with Portugal

The highlight of his Portugal career was lifting the 2016 European Championship, even if he got injured in the final

He never reached a World Cup final and cried after Portugal were knocked out by Spain in the last 16 over the summer

Ironically, his most memorable hour in a Portugal shirt was arguably when he wasn't playing. After getting injured during the 2016 Euros final, he cut such a passionate figure on the touchline, barking instructions to his team-mates, that he had practically taken over from manager Fernando Santos.

However, his dream of winning a World Cup always eluded him, and his best results were reaching the semi-finals in 2006 in Germany and the quarters in 2022 in Qatar.

His final act in football's greatest tournament was Portugal's 1-0 defeat by arch-rivals Spain at this summer's World Cup – a devastating day which saw him leave in tears.

And his final minutes in a Portugal shirt came against Wales in September, when he played 67 minutes in a 1-0 Nations League win over Wales.

After being left on the bench for their subsequent match against Norway, Ronaldo had a row with manager Jesus and flew away from Portugal's camp via his private jet.

Marking his retirement, he wrote: 'To the people of Portugal, the day has come to return the number 7 jersey of our national team. I never felt it was exclusively mine. But for 23 years, I had the privilege and the responsibility to wear it, to defend it, and to take it with me to stadiums all over the world.

'Today has come the moment to hand it over to the future. It was not an easy decision, because some decisions are not made just with the head, they are also made with the heart.

'I was always demanding of myself. I always wanted more, I always believed we could go further. And I gave everything I had for this jersey. There were perfect afternoons and nights, there were victories I will never forget.

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner admitted he had at times 'failed' but was still proud

His time with Portugal in the last international break ended acrimoniously as he abandoned their camp after being left on the bench against Norway

Manager Jorge Jesus insisted that Ronaldo is welcome back, and did his team-mates

'There were defeats that even today I find hard to remember. I also failed, I also suffered, there were also moments when I was not able to give the Portuguese people what they so desired. But I never gave up. And above all, I never stopped feeling proud to represent Portugal.

'Throughout these years, I learned very simple things. Goals pass, trophies stay in museums, records end up being broken. But there is something that time can never erase: the place we occupy in people's hearts.

'If I ever made you happy, if ever a goal of mine made you hug someone, forget a problem, or simply feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it. Because being Portuguese is also that. We suffer together, we get up together.

'If I got this far, it was because we were always hand in hand. And to the Portuguese, to all Portuguese people scattered around the world, I want to tell you one last thing. There will be questions over the way Ronaldo's international career has ended – to the public, it appears to be on rather bitter terms.

Ronaldo was livid after being left on the bench despite warming-up for Portugal's Nations League win over Norway on September 27 – the first time he has been an unused substitute during his 18-year international career.

That led to him skipping three training sessions and abandoning the camp for Portugal's last two matches of the international break, fleeing to Spain via private jet.

The 41-year-old has scored scored 146 goals in 234 games - the most of anybody ever

He did not even watch their next match against Norway because he was soaring away on his plane with his family.

The former Manchester United star was vexed at how Jesus had handled his press conference after leaving him on the bench.

Ronaldo insisted that Jesus had broken a promise to apologise to the 'Portuguese people' and his team-mates for not bringing him on.

He claimed he had been guaranteed 30 minutes of football against Norway after the Portuguese FA persuaded him not to retire following the World Cup.

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner even offered to retire if that was what the coach and head of Portuguese FA wanted, only for them to reiterate their desire to have him.

But most hurtfully, Ronaldo released a stinging 1,996-word statement accusing Jesus of 'broken promises'. He said the manager had agreed to deliver an eight-point mea culpa taking responsibility for leaving him on the bench after a supposed pact to play him.

It was a messy episode – not unlike how he left Manchester United for a second time in 2022 – and the question remains as to whether he would have still been playing had the row never occurred.

#1036. AI-assisted dying? Doris Dörrie's new film addresses prospect of care robots

While the world debates the dangers of artificial intelligence, filmmaker Doris Dörrie explores how humanoid robots could change the way we deal with aging, caregiving and how people choose to die.

Hamburg in the near future: Instead of human drivers, robots deliver parcels. In cafes, robots roll between the tables, serving diners. On the streets, one encounters humanoid robots walking dogs — or the other way around, people taking their robot dogs for a walk.

This is the setting of Doris Dörrie's new film, "Frau Winkler verlässt das Haus" ("Mrs. Winkler Leaves the House"). At the core of the plot is an elderly woman who can no longer live on her own after a fall. With her only daughter unable to provide permanent care, the solution seems simple enough: a care robot with a built-in EOL program, or "End of Life" mode. This robot not only assists with everyday life but can also provide assisted dying under certain conditions, namely when the person explicitly wishes to end their life and meets the relevant medical criteria.

Dörrie's film tackles several major social issues with remarkable lightness. These include the challenges facing aging societies such as Germany, Japan and China, the question of dying on one's own terms and a mother-daughter relationship that raises questions of guilt and responsibility. Even though the story is set in Germany, such issues resonate globally.

"I write about what personally moves and interests me," Dörrie told DW.

One of the best-known contemporary German film directors, Dörrie achieved her breakthrough in 1985 with the comedy "Men…" She gained further international recognition with films such as 2008's "Cherry Blossoms" and "Greetings from Fukushima" (2016).

Assisted suicide is one of the most complex ethical questions of our time. Laws vary around the world. Though some countries permit active euthanasia under certain conditions, others prohibit and criminalize all forms of assisted dying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In her film, Dörrie asks what happens when artificial intelligence begins calculating the cost of caring for an elderly person and weighing whether that cost is still "worth" bearing for society.

The underlying idea isn't new, Dörrie said, pointing to the Japanese legend of Narayama, which is also mentioned in the film. According to the legend, the eldest children were responsible for taking their ageing parents to a mountain and leaving them there to die because there was not enough food for everyone. "And that's also the debate we are currently facing to a certain extent: Can we really afford to let older people live longer and longer?"

In Dörrie's film, elderly people are allowed to make their own decisions once they reach a certain state of health — but they can't change their minds afterwards. Yet what does it really mean to make a decision freely? "It's a tricky situation," says Dörrie, because the question is to what extent one is also pressured into making this decision, "not only because it makes more economic sense, but also because one is no longer a burden on one's loved ones — in this case, one's daughter..."

The film often raises these questions indirectly and with plenty of dark humor. At one point, a care adviser presents the EOL feature to Mrs. Winkler as an attractive and, above all, straightforward additional option, making it sound as though there would be nothing more for her to worry about.

Dörrie is not interested in demonizing AI in her film — quite the opposite. In the film, the care robot, which Mrs. Winkler names Pavlovich, helps the elderly woman rediscover some of her zest for life and get out of the house.

"When you travel through Germany, you see small houses everywhere, and statistics show that an elderly person lives alone in every other house," Dörrie said. "If AI can help in these circumstances, why not use it?" She said she sought to explore this ambiguity in her film. Dividing things into black and white would neither be interesting nor, in her view, accurate.

Dörrie and her crew were surprised during filming by how quickly people can develop emotional bonds with robots. She attributes this to the human brain. "We regard anything that moves and speaks as a living being. We can't help it," she explains. And that is precisely what we need to pay attention to when interacting with AI, Dörrie says. "How often are we truly aware that we are talking to a machine rather than a living being? These are things we still have to learn."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As AI develops, it seems that the boundaries between humans and machines are becoming increasingly blurred. That is precisely why we need to talk about it, Doris Dörrie says. In her view, things become problematic "when we can no longer distance ourselves from technology and stop forming our own thoughts."

Human beings need to ask who we are and what truly defines us, Dörrie said. "I believe there is a major difference between robots and us, and that is the ability to play. A robot might be able to initiate a game, she explains, "but play itself is something profoundly human because it has no particular meaning or purpose."

Alongside these philosophical questions about what it means to be human, Dörrie makes a clear call for AI regulation. "At some point, we had to discuss nuclear weapons internationally, too. We've talked about all kinds of issues in the past, and we haven't just talked about them — we've also managed to find solutions," she points out.

"And I believe we need to move very quickly on this, too," Dörrie said.

This article was originally written in German.

The Argentine strikes the left post and Liverpool will have the chance to book their place in the quarter-finals with their next penalty.

The German makes no mistake, sending Penders the wrong way and putting it into the bottom right corner.

The Belgian calmly steps up and sends Mamardashvili the wrong way, putting into the right corner of the net.

The Dutchman scored Liverpool’s equaliser from the spot and smashes this one into the bottom left corner, with Penders going the wrong way.

He scored during the game and finds the net again. Mamardashvili goes the right way but the penalty from Rogers is very good, going right into the bottom left corner.

Again, Penders guesses the right way but, like Mac Allister, Isak lifts it brilliantly into the top of the net.

The Portuguese finds the net and we are all square after one penalty each.

Penders went the right way but Mac Allister lifts it over the Chelsea keeper.

They will be taken at The Kop. Chelsea goalkeeper Penders disappeared down the tunnel after the full-time whistle and re-emerges with a towel, potentially some penalty-saving notes as well?

Liverpool will take first and it will be Mac Allister who steps up first...

The final whistle is blown so we go to penalties at Anfield.

Looks like we are heading for penalties and if you are looking for omens... Liverpool and Chelsea have had four shootouts in the past: Liverpool won them all - the 2007 Champions League semi-final, the 2019 European Super Cup final, the 2022 League Cup final and the 2022 FA Cup Final.

A word on VAR (again). Watching this competition without the presence of the joy-killing invention is liberating. An occassional decision might get missed but, in the long term, you could live with that if meant you didn’t hear the words “it’s being checked by Stockley Park”. The decision just before, when Florian Wirtz’s shot touched Levi Colwill’s hand, was a case in point. It wasn’t a penalty but VAR being brought into play might convince you it was. Let’s get rid of it, please.

Double change for Liverpool as Isak and Mac Allister replace Ngumoha and Nyoni.

Huge double block from Chelsea and how have Liverpool not scored? Tsimikas’ cross to the back post is headed back across the six-yard box to find Wirtz, who you think is going to score but Colwill makes the block. Then Barcola has a shot blocked by Acheampong.

It is full time at both Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light, where Crystal Palace and Sunderland have booked their places in the League Cup quarter-finals.

Tsimikas gives it away inside his own half and Chelsea counter. Neto drives inside and finds Rogers, who skips past Gomez. Rogers then finds the overlapping Palestra on the left side of the box and the Italian is denied by Mamardashvili at his near post.

Manchester City have just beaten Brighton 4-3 on penalties whilst on the south coast Bournemouth have comfortably beaten Aston Villa 3-0. Both sides are into the hat for tonight’s quarter-final draw.

Lavia cynically brings down Ngumoha as the Liverpool forward drove through the Chelsea half and is correctly booked.

Liverpool are taking off Van Dijk and Jacquet is coming on in his place. No injury for Van Dijk.

What a terrific cup tie this has been. It helps when there is an edge between the sides and you can feel the tension in the air. What has been noticeable in the last three games at Anfield, though, is the change in the atmosphere. Slowly but surely the locals are buying into what Andoni Iraola is trying to achieve. Liverpool could lose this game tonight by going all out to win it but there is a clearly identity developing that makes you think they are starting to get on the right lines.

After Gakpo fouls Lavia, Chelsea have a free-kick just over 25 yards out. Rogers lines it up but his effort is terrible, flying into The Kop.

Chelsea are going to make a triple change. Palestra, Barco and Emegha come on, with the latter on for his Chelsea debut. Gusto, Caicedo and Welbeck head off.

Good save from Penders. The ball comes to Barcola outside the Chelsea penalty area. The Frenchman drives inside before getting his shot away from the edge of the box. The shot takes a small deflection and Penders does well to make the save down to his left.

The game between Manchester City and Brighton at The Etihad has ended 2-2, therefore it has now gone to penalties.

Chances at both ends. Gomez whips in a cross from the right and picks out Araujo in the centre of the box but the Uruguayan’s powerful header is straight at Penders. He probably should have scored.

Then Chelsea counter and Rogers is in acres of space. His shot from just outside the box takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner, which comes to nothing.

Gusto’s behaviour in recent minutes has been appalling. First he went down after virtually no contact from Van Dijk and now goes down again, once more not a foul. He shows his boot to the linesman as if it came off in a challenge from Barcola but the replays show that his boot did not come off and he was attempting to con the officials.

Andoni Iraola is turning to his bench for the first time tonight and makes a double substitution as Wirtz and Barcola replace McConnell and Koumas. Some double change that for Liverpool!

Fascinating to watchg Trey Nyoni and the responsibility he has taken on his shoulders. He’s only 19 but those who have worked with him since he arrived at Liverpool as a 16-year-old will tell you he has a maturity of someone in their mid-twenties. He has tried to get on the ball and play, he’s been strong when it’s been required and always been in the right place to get a foot in. He’s going to play a lot of games for Liverpool if he maintains this trajectory.

Achemapong scythes Ngumoha down as the latter cut inside and the former is correctly booked.

Down on the south coast, Bournemouth appear to be cruising into the quarter-finals as Alvaro Rodriguez has put them 3-0 up against Aston Villa.

Should Rogers have done better there? In fortuitous circumstances, he is played through but he does not show the conviction to drive towards the Liverpool penalty area. His touch lets him and the ball rolls through to Mamardashvili.

Moments later, Rogers forces Mamadrashvili into a save to his left and the Liverpool players are furious that a handball was not given. It clearly hit Rogers’ arm before he shot but Chelsea do have the corner. Chelsea play it short before eventually Henderson swings it in before Araujo heads away.

We are back under way at Anfield. No changes from either side at the break.

Manchester City have equalised at home against Brighton, with Rayan Cherki’s free-kick from just outside the box taking a big deflection off his teammate Vitor Reis and ending up in the back ot the Brighton net.

Manchester City 1 Brighton 2 (70’)Bournemouth 2 Aston Villa 0 (58’)Fulham 0 Crystal Palace 1 (56’)Sunderland 3 Brentford 1 (56’)Liverpool 1 Chelsea 1 HT

Bournemouth have doubled their advantage against Aston Villa through Lewis Cook just over five minutes into the second half.

Possession: Liverpool 50%-50% ChelseaShots: 6-2Shots on target: 2-1Corners: 5-0Touches in opposition box: 5-9

The first half is brought to an end at Anfield and the game is level at 1-1 going into the break. Rogers put Chelsea in front from the spot only for Gakpo to also score a penalty moments later to equalise for Liverpool.

The outswinging corner is sent in from the left but Araujo’s header goes over the bar. Meanwhile, Lacroix is slowly limping his way around the pitch to the tunnel and is moving very gingerly, which could suggest an extended period on the sidelines.

As we enter three minutes of added time, Colwill replaces the injured Lacroix.

Liverpool can sense a second goal. First, Gakpo has a shot saved by Penders before Ngumoha wins the hosts a corner. Before that is taken, play has been stopped as Lacroix is down clutching at his left hamstring.

Not a murmur from Xabi Alonso as his side take the lead. The penalty Morgan Rogers dispatched went in the same corner as Alonso picked in the 2007 Champions League semi-final and perhaps he had a sense of what was coming as Liverpool are now level and it’s a fair reflection of how an intriguing opening 45 minutes has played out. It really wouldn’t be a surprise if we need spot-kicks to separate these teams at 90 minutes.

Like Rogers moments ago, Gakpo sends the goalkeeper the wrong way and puts the penalty away to equalise. Gakpo slots into the bottom left corner in front of The Kop and the Dutchman continues his fine scoring record in this competition. Both sides have been gifted penalties and both teams take advantage.

Cody Gakpo slots home a penalty to equalise for Liverpool against Chelsea! 💪 https://t.co/rS775LH0Gb

Like London buses, two penalties come in quick succession. From a Liverpool corner out on the left, Fofana is penalised for a handball and the referee has no choice but to point to the spot. The Chelsea players protest but it clearly hit Fofana’s arm, which was above his head.

Rogers sends Mamardashvili the wrong way and puts Chelsea 1-0 up in front of their travelling supporters. It was a quality penalty from Rogers, who deposited it into the right corner of the goal. It is a gift for Chelsea, who did not look like scoring but are gifted a chance to score through that silly Gravenberch challenge.

Morgan Rogers puts Chelsea in front against Liverpool from the spot! 🎯 https://t.co/ocMXFNCW9F

Caicedo goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area and the referee points to the spot. It is a silly and needless challenge from Gravenberch, who slides into the back of Caicedo and gives the referee no choice but to give a penalty. Not that it would be overturned but there is no VAR anyway.

Ex-Liverpool man Henderson was holding the ball for a while but now hands over to Rogers to take...

They are into the second half at Manchester and Brighton have retaken the lead through Georginio Rutter. Brighton now lead Manchester City 2-1.

That is a gift from Chelsea. The communication at the back between Gusto and Fofana is poor, with the former playing a poor pass backwards looking for Fofana, who cannot reach it and the ball rolls behind for the easiest of corners for Liverpool in front of The Kop.

Gakpo takes an outswinging corner but Welbeck is on hand to head away at the front post.

We are yet to see the first goal of the night at Anfield but they are flying in at the Stadium of Light. Brentford have pulled a goal back against Sunderland through Callum Wilson and it is now 3-1 in the north east.

Chelsea want a penalty. Rogers goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area under a challenge from Araujo but it was a fair shoulder-to-shoulder challenge and that is not a penalty.

At the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in dreamland. Malick Fofana has put them 3-0 up against Brentford closing in on half-time.

A wasted free kick from Chelsea, and goodness, Austin McPhee is not happy. Chelsea’s set piece coach was up on the touchline, remonstrating to nobody in particular but it was obvious to see the frustration that the plan he has worked on - a chip to the side, a cutback into the middle - has fallen down at the first attempt. To compound his fury, McPhee just blew a gasket after Chelsea were not awarded a penalty following a coming together between Ronald Araujo and Morgan Rogers.

Tsimikas has let Ngumoha down there. Ngumoha does brilliantly to dribble through two Chelsea defenders around the halfway line and drives down the left. He then plays the ball outside to Tsimikas, who should do so much better with his cross but picks out the front-post defender Lacroix.

Meanwhile at Craven Cottage, Crystal Palace have taken the lead at Fulham thanks to Eddie Nketiah.

McConnell becomes the second Liverpool player to be booked tonight for handball. He lost the ball on halfway and cynically handled the ball as Rogers attempted to counter. A fairly clear-cut booking for McConnell there.

A reminder that there is no VAR tonight and if the game is level after 90 minutes, we will go straight to penalties. Referee Darren England has summoned Chelsea captain Caicedo and former Liverpool midfielder Henderson over for a word.

Caicedo puts Tsimikas’ cross from the left behind for the first corner of the night. Gakpo sends in the inswinger but the whistle goes as Chelsea are awarded a free-kick for a foul from Tsimikas on Gusto.

There has yet to be a goal at Anfield but at the Stadium of Light Sunderland have doubled their lead over Brentford courtesy of Tymur Tutierov’s goal.

The first booking of the night at Anfield goes the way of the home side. Koumas slides in to try and block a clearance from Lacroix and is booked. Koumas barely touched Lacroix and that is never a yellow card.

Meanwhile, in the north east, Sunderland have taken the lead against Brentford through Chemsdine Talbi.

Brighton had led in Manchester but the home side have just equalised. Mateo Kovacic has scored from range to bring Manchester City level with five minutes to go in the first half.

Clear to see in these early exchanges that Cody Gakpo has been deployed as Liverpool’s main “striker” with Lewis Koumas, James McConnell - who played in the 2024 final when Liverpool beat Chelsea 1-0 - and Rio Ngumoha operating in behind him. Jordan Henderson seems to be the man whom Xabi Alonso wants to trigger Chelsea’s press. They are playing a rigid 4-5-1 formation but, this being Alonso, the system is always flexible. His ethos is to be able to play two or three systems in a game if needed.

Ngumoha drives at Neto down Liverpool’s left and is felled by the Portuguese forward. It is an obvious free-kick and Neto is a touch fortunate not to be booked for that blatant foul. Ngumoha, who was fantastic for Liverpool against Villarreal in the Champions League just over a week ago, already into the action.

Tsimikas clips in the delivery but it is headed away by Lacroix.

The second goal in the League Cup this evening has come in Manchester and has gone the way of the away side. Malick Yalcouye has put Brighton in front against Manchester City on the half-hour mark.

We are under way at Anfield. Who will book their place in the League Cup quarter-finals; Liverpool or Chelsea?

Jordan Henderson is busily going around geeing up Chelsea’s players, in exactly the same fashion as he did when he played in this stadium for 12 years. He got an ovation here in May, when Brentford drew 1-1, that left him extremely emotional but it remains to be seen what will happen when he gets his first touch this evening. There has been no acknowledgement - yet - from The Kop and the same is true for Xabi Alonso. But, then again, why would there be when there is such lingering enmity between these clubs?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off at Anfield. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Has come on the south coast, where Bournemouth have taken the lead against Aston Villa courtesy of Amine Adli’s goal inside the opening 10 minutes.

“The cups are important for us this year. For sure, we face today a good challenge, coming to Anfield, and we want to be in the next round. It is another competition. We know it is another format, it is make-or-break, so we want to make it happen today with a great performance.

“From the beginning we have taken it seriously. We have a tough game and we want to have a good feeling that we are competing. We have to do many great things. In one game there can be many little games with the energy created. These players have played here before. We have practiced penalties but sometimes it is about the feeling of the day.”

The games at the Vitality Stadium, Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light have just begun. That means four of the five ties tonight have started, with just the game at Anfield to begin in just over 10 minutes.

At The Etihad, Manchester City have kicked off against Brighton. Then, there are three 7.45pm kick-offs before Liverpool begin against Chelsea at Anfield at 8pm.

More than two years have passed since Rio Ngumoha chose to leave Chelsea for Liverpool, but the frustration remains at Stamford Bridge. The pain of losing a player of Ngumoha’s potential does not pass quickly, especially as the winger was part of Chelsea’s academy system for eight years. It must sting to see a London boy, one of their own, now delighting the Anfield crowd.

For many at Chelsea, the anger at Ngumoha’s departure in 2024 will probably never subside. Or, at least, it will not subside while he continues to develop so thrillingly at Liverpool. Such was Chelsea’s annoyance at the time of his exit, Telegraph Sport reported last year, Liverpool’s scouts were subsequently banned from attending matches at their academy centre.

All five games this evening are all-Premier League ties:

Manchester City vs Brighton 7.30pmBournemouth vs Aston Villa 7.45pmFulham vs Crystal Palace 7.45pmSunderland vs Brentford 7.45pmLiverpool vs Chelsea 8pm

The two sides already into the hat for the quarter-finals are Bradford and Fleetwood, who knocked Arsenal out last night. The draw for the quarter-finals will take place after tonight’s matches.

Tonight's Blues. ✊💙 #CFC | #CarabaoCup https://t.co/Q7pTQHkgDc

Come on you Reds ✊🔴 https://t.co/o9Rc2yjV7c

It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso said. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

#1032. Mysterious anthrax outbreak kills hippos in Africa — raising concerns for human spread

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Hippos in Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have been affected by an anthrax outbreak over the past month.Credit: Evelyn Hockstein/MCT/Tribune News Service via Getty

An anthrax outbreak has killed at least 30 hippopotamuses in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in the past month. No cases in people have been reported so far, but authorities say they are monitoring the situation closely.

The dead animals were first found in September in Virunga National Park in eastern DRC, and laboratory tests confirmed they died from anthrax, a serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis.

The outbreak comes at the same time as health authorities and conservation groups in the DRC manage large outbreaks of Ebola and cholera, and the ongoing humanitarian challenges caused by armed conflict in the region. A disease outbreak of anthrax in wildlife puts further pressure on already limited resources, say researchers.

The anthrax bacterium is found naturally in soil worldwide and can infect livestock and wild animals if they encounter its spores. Officials at Virunga National Park said in a statement that teams have been monitoring the affected area and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses and there have been no new mortalities in the past two weeks.

David Hayman, a disease ecologist at Massey University in Palmerston North, New Zealand, says the main risk to people is from handling infected carcasses or consuming contaminated meat. The disease can be treated with antibiotics if caught early, but it can be fatal without treatment.

Although no cases have been reported in people during this outbreak, Charity Mutesi, an epidemiologist at the Uganda National Institute of Public Health in Kampala, says that infections can go undetected because people might decide to stay at home rather than going to a clinic for treatment. People often use herbs on the lesions caused by some anthrax infections, or might seek care from drug shops, private clinics or traditional healers, who do not report the cases to the national disease surveillance systems, she adds.

The DRC has experienced several anthrax outbreaks in animals and people over the past few years. In March 2025, an outbreak killed around 65 hippos. Fifteen people tested positive for the disease in bordering Uganda, two of whom died.

“It is very concerning that these outbreaks continue to happen,” says Ricardo Soares Magalhães, an epidemiologist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.

#1030. Tragic Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel's family say they have an 'impossible void to fill' as his dad is comforted with devastated loved ones arriving at his funeral

Published: 07:14 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 08:52 EDT, 5 November 2026

Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel's family have said they have an 'impossible void to fill' as hundreds of people gathered to pay their respects after he was killed in a freak mid-match collision with a goalkeeper.

Mourners filled the streets of De Miguel’s hometown of Navahermosa in the foothills of Montes de Toledo, outside Toledo, where he was born and his family still live.

The 30-year-old Tenerife striker’s death after the on-pitch incident has stunned football-obsessed Spain and hundreds of members of the public turned out alongside his family and friends outside the parish church of San Miguel Arcángel.

The town came to a standstill in the early afternoon with police shutting down the roads nearby to cars to prepare for the ceremony.

Mourners gathered outside the 16th century Baroque church shortly before 2.30pm local time with the warm sun and blue sky providing a contrast to the sombre mood inside the town.

His sister Marta wiped away tears as she arrived at the church alongside family.

De Miguel’s girlfriend Maria and their one-year-old daughter Carla, parents and grandparents were expected to attend alongside team-mates and directors of the Canary Islands club.

The family released a statement this morning about their shock.

Seaking on their behalf, Manuel Hernandez said: ‘Jesus leaves a void that is impossible to fill, but also an immense memory in all of us who have been lucky enough to share our lives with him.

The father of tragic footballer Jesus de Miguel is consoled at the 30-year-old's funeral

Tenerife coach Alvaro Cervera arrives at the funeral in the striker's hometown of Navahermosa

Mourners gather in Navahermosa to pay respects to tragic Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel

#1029. Formula One in Rwanda: Sportswashing claims vs. hopes for African legacy

Formula One will return to Africa for the first time since 1993. There is concern Rwanda are using it as another sportswashing opportunity, but there is also hope the event's legacy can impact wider African society.

Rwanda's sports portfolio has grown after confirming it will host Formula One races from the early 2030s. The track is to be built in Bugesera near Kigali International Airport, which Qatar Airways, an F1 sponsor, owns 60% of.

"To be an African and to see it happening in real time, for me in my lifetime because Kyalami [the track in South Africa where F1 was last hosted in Africa] was before I was born, I'm more than happy to have it on the continent," South African presenter and content creator Nqobile Khwezi told Sky Sports.

"To be able to give that taste back to the rest of the world and the audience of Formula One would be an absolute delight."

F1 have also highlighted the benefits for the host nation.

"Through this race we have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to our more than 100 million fans across Africa and firmly believe that sport can be a positive force for good," an F1 spokesperson told The Athletic.

DW contacted Rwanda's Ministry of Sports for comment, but did not receive a promised reply.

For the country's President, Paul Kagame, another move into sport is hardly a surprise given his ventures into European football and the NBA in recent years. Rwanda even sponsored Bayern Munich, but fan and media backlash over the deal caused the Bundesliga club to drop the commercial element with the country's tourist arm, Visit Rwanda, last year.

With many critics accusing Kagame and Rwanda of sportswashing, the arrival of F1, a sport valued at approximately $34 billion (€30 billion), according to sports business website Sportico, brings fresh questions.

"This deal may have positive economic and social impacts across Africa, but we should be realistic about circumstances on the ground in Rwanda," Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told DW.

"Human Rights Watch wrote to Formula One in February 2025 to ask how it is addressing the human rights impacts of its activities, including regarding Rwanda and other countries’ bid to host a F1 Grand Prix. We did not receive a response," said Mudge, adding that F1 should only approve racing in the country after addressing the human rights impacts of hosting a race there.

"Rwanda, like other countries, has also used high-profile sports deals and races in the past to distract from its abysmal human rights record. Rwanda is currently the power behind the abusive M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and its military forces have been implicated in unlawful displacement and deaths of civilians in violation of international humanitarian law."

For Mohamed Keita, returning the sport to Africa is overdue, but the choice of country is telling.

"The fact that F1 excluded the world's second largest continent from its race series for three decades is indefensible in its own right and is actually a stain on a sport which claims to be global," Keita, Senior Policy Officer, Africa, at the Human Rights Foundation told DW.

"The choice of Rwanda, however, is deeply controversial," Keita continued. "Rwanda is a brutal dictatorship. Its regime is under partial US sanctions for its military occupations of territories of eastern DRC. Rwanda is arming and financing a militia involved in rapes, massacres, forced recruitment and violent plunder of natural resources."

Formula One has history on the continent. In 1958, there was a race in Morocco and more recently, in South Africa, where the last F1 race in Africa took place at the Kyalami racetrack in Johannesburg in 1993. Many previous races in the country were overshadowed by the policy of apartheid.

Despite Rwanda securing the deal first, South Africa believes it will host before them. When Rwanda announced their hosting, South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa sent his congratulations in a social media post, adding: "This contract is a recognition of the capabilities of the Rwandan nation and of our continent more broadly."

South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie also congratulated Rwanda, but pivotally added that South Africa "will get F1, even before 2030."

There is no denying that hosting a race in South Africa would cost significantly less time and money, given the existing infrastructure.

In either country, comes a legacy opportunity. Sports such as Formula One, where the majority of decision-makers, drivers, team principles and engineers are white men, are a living example of the unlevel playing field. The hope of racing in Africa is that it will go some way to changing that.

"I think that's the kind of aspirational drive of hosting a Formula 1 race. It's leveraging STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] education, technology, aspiring young girls or women, leveling the playing fields, if it's for all those other reasons and we can make it work then I say yes to Formula 1 in Africa," Dr. Kamilla Swart-Arries, an expert in South Africa's events industry and the legacy of sports events, told DW in 2024.

"I hope F1 will consider further investment in developing African talent in motorsport," said Keita. "There's a lot of good that F1 can do if it genuinely wants to grow the sport in Africa, but Rwanda does not make sense at this moment unless you're doing it purely for the benefit of one dictator and the beauty of the hilly terrain."

"The proposition here is to take the world's most expensive sport to Rwanda, which is one of the world's poorest countries. Rwanda is consistently listed among the UN's list of the 25 least developed countries in the world," said Keita.

The return of the fastest show in sports is a huge moment for both Rwanda and Africa. It raises questions about President Kagame's use of sport, but it also offers an opportunity to shape the event's legacy. Unlike the race Rwanda wants to host, this is not about being the fastest but about making the most of the chance.
